title: Inheritance in practice
hookLine: fixed shares for family, and up to a third by will

lines: A THIRD, AND A THIRD IS A LOT.
cards: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas lies sick in Mecca, sure he is about to die. He has some wealth and one daughter to inherit from him.
The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ comes to visit, and Sa'd asks straight out: may I give all my wealth away in charity? It sounds like a beautiful question. The Prophet says no.
Then half? No. Then a third?
A third, the Prophet answers, and a third is a lot. Tradition says Sa'd recovered. But that bedside bargain became a line in Islamic law.

teach.h: LAYER ONE: SHARES FIXED IN SURAH FOUR.
teach.b: Islamic inheritance works in two layers. The first is fixed by the Qur'an. In surah four, God names the shares: what children receive, what parents receive, what a husband or wife receives.
The verses call them an ordinance from God, and the jurists built a whole science around them, called fara'id, the obligatory shares. You don't choose these. The second layer is yours.

teach.h: LAYER TWO: A WILL, UP TO A THIRD.
teach.b: Before the shares are divided, the debts are paid and the will is carried out, and the will can reach up to a third of what is left.
That third is where a person can remember a friend, a cause, a mosque, a stranger who was kind.

One limit: a report in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi says there is no bequest to an heir. Those who already have a share from the Qur'an can't be given extra by will; the third is for people the shares don't reach.
And the Prophet gave Sa'd a reason.

teach.h: LEAVE THEM WELL OFF, NOT DEPENDENT.
teach.b: In Sahih al-Bukhari, he says leaving your heirs well off is better than leaving them dependent, holding out their hands to people. So the limit isn't a limit on generosity.

It points generosity two ways at once: to family, through the shares, and to the wider world, through the third. A family may sit with a scholar to work out the exact shares, and the schools disagree on some rarer cases.
But the shape holds: the debts, the third, then the shares.

how: When a Muslim dies, debts are paid first, then any will of up to a third is carried out, and the rest is divided among family members by the shares set out in surah four, often with a scholar's help.

o: whatever the one who died wrote in a will, without limit
fixed family shares from the Qur'an, plus up to a third by will
an equal split of the estate among all the children

games.q: inheritance in practice — tap the pairs.

s: in Islamic law a person can leave everything to charity by will
a will can reach up to a third; the rest goes to the family by fixed shares.
debts are paid before the shares are divided
debts first, then the will, then the shares.
a will can give extra to someone who already inherits a share
a report says there is no bequest to an heir; the third is for others.

games.q: you're Sa'd, sick and sure you're dying, with one daughter to inherit. you ask the Prophet to let you give your wealth away in charity. what does he allow?
o: all of it, since charity is good.
a third, and he says a third is a lot.
games.why: he refuses all and half, allows a third, and says leaving heirs well off is better than leaving them dependent.

practice: Write a very simple will, only in your head for now: start with what you owe, anyone you'd want paid back, any promise you'd want kept.
Then think about your third, not the money but the people outside your family: a teacher, a neighbor, a place that fed you once. Hold one name, and if it feels right, you can write it down later.

wordCard.voice: Inheritance in practice. Fixed shares for the family from the Qur'an, and up to a third by will for those the shares don't reach. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the obligatory shares; the science of dividing an inheritance.

carryVoice: Your line: a third by will. Family through the shares, the wider world through the third. See you tomorrow.
